en: Could anyone bring grief?
Should this honorable khan's family
Have had to flee to Bukhara?
When she has fled here of her own will,
Could anyone bring her grief?
Yesterday, in the valley of Jylgynduu,
Along the broad Talas,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz headed for the valley
And made their camps;
Kumys by day, girls by night—
Such were their pleasures then.
With armor no bullet could pierce
Set upon their brows, the many Kyrgyz
Swaggered in those days.
Ruling the Nogai as well,
Stirring up the whole world,
They lived in delight.
Yesterday, on their wrists, sharp steel
Hung at the ready;
United across the world,
They lived in delight.
Yesterday, in Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
The multitude of Kyrgyz lay encamped.
Below Tört-Kül,
In the garden Prince Manas planted,
Kanykei's white palace stood,
Its doors of iron and solid tin.
Though a woman, that unfortunate one's
Prosperity far surpassed the rest.
Many hurried to her door;
Unless the guards gave them leave,
No mortal rushed in rashly.
When she said, 'Speak!' to the world,
If she suddenly gave an order,
Sixty would rush to carry it out.
Human noses and ears—
Alas, they wore them as amulets.
No one dared approach;
Those they encountered did not survive.
Warriors who advanced stood amazed;
Unable to go near, mortals wandered helplessly.
Such was the life Kanykei led
While saintly Manas was alive.
My saintly child Kanykei
Was a khan as great as a mountain.
Had you seen Kanykei's prosperity,
It was so very great.
Among round-headed mortals,
My dear foal was a blessed soul.
Better, then, good people,
Let us send word to the nation.
If the people agree,
Eight hundred households of subjects
Let us place under her hand.
Here in Bukhara,
Let us raise her as khan.
Making Kanykei our support,
Here in Bukhara,
Let us bring prosperity.
To Alty-Shaar and Margalang,
As far down as Samarkand,
Let us send a stern command.
Six thousand otter pelts, a thousand ingots—
Let us exact the tribute firmly,
Let us gather gold in earnest.
Let none call her a fallen woman;
Let us silence the people's mouths.
To make this decision firm,
From Alty-Shaar, Kokon and Margalang,
Let us gather the elders.
Let no bird of prey eat this swan;
This child of mine standing here—
Let none call her a wretched woman;
Let us silence the people's mouths.
Let no bird of prey eat this goose;
This child of mine standing here—
Let none call her a fugitive woman;
Let us silence the people's mouths.
Here in Bukhara,
Let us send out firm word;
Though my child is a woman,
Let us raise her as lord.
Such is the command Allah has written;
Let us accept it as it is.
This year he is still a cradle babe.
When her son reaches twelve,
Let us hold Manas's memorial feast.
Let us speak this in God's name,
Make our promise firm,
Swear an oath binding unto death,
And chew white wheat flour.
To allow no excuses,
Let us hold the holy Quran.
The orphan entrusted to our care—
When he reaches twelve,
Let us send word to the people.
The khans throughout the earth—
Let us gather them all,
And hold a worthy, splendid feast.
Manas, who has gone to the other world—
Let us strive to give his spirit true contentment.
Let us put my golden crown upon him,
And seat the dear child on a golden throne.
Let us send out firm word
And raise this son of his as khan.
When he reaches fifteen,
Let us obey his wishes.
Men skilled with the spear—
Let us give him a thousand of them.
Strong men who wield the battle-axe—
Let us give him a thousand of them.
Marksmen who never miss—
Let us give him a thousand of them.
Turning our thoughts nowhere else,
In his father Manas's place,
Let us make the boy our ruler.
Alty-Shaar and broad Bukhara—
Let us obey his wishes.
If he marches to war against Kakan,
Let us stand as the boy's support.
Good men, into great Beijing, looming dark,
Let us march straight and thrust our spears.
Manas, who has passed from this world—
Thus let us avenge him.
Beijing, beyond even the four caliphs' reach—
Let us discover its strength and condition.
Khan Manas was brought down;
For this son he left behind,
Let us, poor souls, stand as support.'
As Temir Khan spoke,
'The prince's household
Has come here in flight,' they said.
Hearing it, the multitude grieved.
To the city of Temir Khan,
Your sister-in-law came wandering;
The countless riches left by Manas,
Your sister-in-law had scattered when she came.
Finding no place to lie down,
Finding not half a joint of meat,
Finding no horse to mount,
Finding no milk to quench her thirst,
The broad world narrowed around her;
Your stately sister-in-law was humbled.
Exhausted, your sister-in-law could not walk.
Kanykei entered Bukhara in mourning;
Semetey came there in flight.
Kanykei arrived a wanderer;
Semetey arrived an orphan.
Temir Khan gave his command;
When Temir Khan commanded,
His people did not oppose him.
Then the khojas in white turbans,
The mullahs who taught their lessons:
'For this daughter who has come wandering,
Temir Khan has acted wisely,' they said.
'While mighty Manas was alive,
He offended his daughter;
Now he has drawn her to his side
And made her close to him,' they said.
The multitude of Bukhara, ruled by a sovereign,
Once their khan had given his command,
Did not make him say it twice.
'The noble khan's offspring,
Straying and fleeing to Bukhara,
Has come here wandering,' they said.
The people approved his words
And now agreed to his wishes.
There were nine hundred households
Together in Bukhara;
These he now set apart for her.
They now agreed to his wishes;
He now sent word to his people.
Over nine hundred households,
Though a woman, the unfortunate one
They now raised as khan.
They draped her in silk,
Mounted her on a smooth-gaited pacer;
Sixty women, eighty girls—
So many stood about her.
That dear mother of yours, Kanykei,
Had fled to Bukhara.
When first she fled there,
She had lost her fierce warrior,
At the age of thirty-two.
Bereft of Khan Manas,
She saw a night that would not turn back.
To Temir Khan's city
She wandered and made her living.
To the walled city of Bukhara,
Bereaved, she fled and sustained her life.
She saw a moonless night;
Bereft of her precious one,
She lived through days of devastation.
With nine hundred households under her hand,
The people's mouths were silenced.
Kanykei remained in mourning;
Semetey entered Bukhara and was raised there.
Such was the command God had sent;
She now saw it was so.
Without calling the orphan her child,
She gave him wholly to her brother,
To Ismayil.
He never wore a coat draped over his back.
Manas, who had gone to the other world—
He had no idea this was his father.
The dear land called Talas—
He had no idea this was his homeland.
Kanykei, who went in mourning—
He had no idea the poor woman was his mother.
At that time, Semetey,
Temir Khan's dear camel calf,
Ismayil's son,
That orphan left by Manas,
Had his mind on other things.
Many years passed between;
If you looked, the days had passed.
He prospered by plundering riches;
Semetey grew up in Bukhara.
The orphan grew to maturity;
He joined the ranks of men.
No one could torment him;
The bold lad who took after his father—
None remained who could turn him with a catching pole.
He proved a burning ember;
He proved a thundering bullet.
In the great city of Bukhara,
Damn him, no such troublemaker had ever appeared!
When he reached twelve,
He imprisoned any mendicant he saw
And beat the wandering dervishes.
Unable to endure his mischief,
The whole city of Bukhara grew weary.
He proved a lion protected by Shay;
All twelve parts of his body grew in perfect balance.
One day there was turmoil in Bukhara.
The khojas in white turbans,
The mullahs who taught their lessons,
Looked about in fear and grieved.
The reason for their grief was this:
Eighty khojas and a hundred mullahs
He shut inside their mosque.
The notorious troublemaker Semetey
Beat every one alike.
The khojas wept in anguish;
The mullahs' heads were split.
The people of Bukhara took counsel
And ran this way and that.
'I shall die!' they cried, despairing of life.
The people grieved;
Many heads were split.
With their belts around their necks,
They ran in flustered haste;
Their knees bent to the ground.
They ran this way and that,
Following along his path.
He had reached twelve;
